docs.title: Install with Helm
docs.text:
Already installed?

Skip this part if KeenPG is already installed for you.

Install the chart

Run this from the folder that holds the chart. It installs everything: the operator, the console and the console's own database.

Install KeenPG
helm install keenpg ./keenpg-operator -n keenpg-operator --create-namespace

Wait until all pods are Running:

Check the pods
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get pods
Expected output
NAME                                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
keenpgo-7b8d8dcc4f-tjnht            1/1     Running   0          2m
keenpgo-console-6797b94dc-rdl5j     1/1     Running   0          2m
keenpgo-console-db-0                1/1     Running   0          2m

docs.title: Open the console
docs.text:
The console service is only reachable inside Kubernetes. To open it from your browser, change the service to NodePort:

Expose the console
kubectl -n keenpg-operator patch svc keenpgo-console -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get svc keenpgo-console
Expected output
NAME              TYPE       CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)                      AGE
keenpgo-console   NodePort   10.96.120.15   <none>        80:31847/TCP,443:30512/TCP   5m

Open https://<node IP>:<node port>, for example https://192.168.49.2:30512. (On minikube, minikube ip gives the node IP.)

Certificate warning on first visit

The first time, the browser warns that the certificate is not trusted. That is expected: the console made its own certificate. Click Advanced → Continue, or see HTTPS and the certificate.

docs.title: Optional: dashboards and logs
docs.text:
Install these once if you want the Observability › Dashboards page and the Monitoring and Logging switches:

Install monitoring and logging
kubectl apply -k config/monitoring      # Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager
kubectl apply -k config/logging         # Loki, only if you want logs

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Sign-in page

  1. Open the console address in your browser.
  2. Type your username and password, then click Sign In.

The first password

Helm makes a random password for the user admin and keeps it in the Secret keenpgo-console-admin. Read it with:

Read the admin username and password
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo
Example output
admin
x7Rk2pQw9LmZ4vTnB8sD   (yours is different)

To choose the password yourself, add --set console.admin.password='Choose-A-Password-1' to helm install.

The Secret is only read once

It is read when the console starts for the first time and there is no admin yet. After that, the password lives in the console's own database. If you change it in the console, the Secret no longer shows it.

Change the admin password on day one

Click your name (top right) → Change password.

You stay signed in for 12 hours. To sign out, click your name → Sign out.

Reset a forgotten password

Forgot the admin password?

Remove the admin user from the console database and restart the console. It then creates admin again with the password from the Secret above. Other users, the audit log and settings are kept.

flowchart LR
    A["Remove the admin user from the console database"] --> B["Restart the console"]
    B --> C["Console creates admin again with the password from the Secret"]

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    class A,B step
    class C ok
Reset the admin user
kubectl -n keenpg-operator exec keenpgo-console-db-0 -- sh -c "PGPASSWORD=\"\$POSTGRES_PASSWORD\" \$(ls -d /usr/pgsql-*/bin | tail -1)/psql -h /tmp -U keenpgo -d keenpgo -c \"DELETE FROM console_users WHERE username = 'admin';\""
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console

DELETE 1 means it worked.

Other users forgot their password? An admin resets it in Settings → Users (key icon).

docs.title: HTTPS and the certificate
docs.text:
The console always uses HTTPS. It makes its own self-signed certificate the first time it starts, and keeps it in the Secret keenpgo-console-tls.

  • Nothing else is needed: no cert-manager and no extra job. It works the same with Helm, kubectl, Argo CD and OpenShift.
  • Every console pod and every restart uses the same certificate. It is valid for 2 years; the console makes a new one 30 days before it ends.
  • http:// on the same port is sent on to https:// by itself.

Stop the browser warning

Save the certificate and trust it on your computer (it is its own authority):

Save the certificate
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d > keenpg-console.crt

Then trust it on your system:

  • Windows

    1. Double-click the file
    2. Install Certificate
    3. Local Machine
    4. Trusted Root Certification Authorities

  • macOS

    1. Open it in Keychain Access
    2. System
    3. Set Always Trust

  • Linux (Chrome / Firefox)

    1. Browser settings
    2. Certificates
    3. Authorities
    4. Import

Advanced HTTPS setups

Your address in the certificateYour own certificateOpenShiftIngress or load balancer

By default the certificate is for the console's service names and localhost. To add the IP or name people type in the browser, set KEENPGO_TLS_HOSTS and let the console make a new certificate:

kubectl -n keenpg-operator set env deploy/keenpgo-console KEENPGO_TLS_HOSTS=192.168.49.2,console.example.com
kubectl -n keenpg-operator delete secret keenpgo-console-tls
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console

Use this for a certificate from your company's authority or cert-manager.

Put it in the same Secret. The console uses it as it is, never replaces it, and picks up a renewed one within 5 minutes:

kubectl -n keenpg-operator create secret tls keenpgo-console-tls --cert=console.crt --key=console.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console

Create a passthrough Route, so the browser talks HTTPS straight to the console:

oc -n keenpg-operator create route passthrough keenpgo-console --service=keenpgo-console --port=https
oc -n keenpg-operator get route keenpgo-console

Use this when an Ingress or load balancer already does HTTPS.

It can send plain HTTP to the console with the header X-Forwarded-Proto: https; the console accepts that. Or turn the console's own HTTPS off with KEENPGO_TLS=off.

docs.title: The screen layout
docs.text:
Every page has the same frame:

Area What it does Left menu Opens each page. On small screens it shows only icons; click » at the bottom to open it. Pages with an arrow (Observability) open a list of sub-pages. Project (top left) Chooses the project you are working in. All projects (the default) shows the clusters of every project you can see. Create cluster (top right) Starts a new database from any page. Your name (top right) Change your password, manage users (admins only), sign out.

Project list with All projects

Like All namespaces in OpenShift, All projects is first in the list. Pick a project to see only its clusters. The lists of clusters, the SQL editor and Backup & Restore follow the project you pick.

Your role decides what you see

You see only the pages and buttons your role allows. See Users and access.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
The Home page is your daily check: in one look you see whether everything is fine.

Home page

Top card

  • Operator ready 1/1 means the KeenPG operator is running.
  • The chips show the PostgreSQL versions you can use.
  • The four shortcuts open Create cluster, SQL editor, Databases and Migration.

Count cards

Card Meaning Clusters ring All clusters, split by state. Healthy Clusters with every pod ready. Need attention Clusters with a problem. Open them first. Being created New clusters that are still starting. Kubernetes health Problems in Kubernetes itself, for example a node that is not ready.

Your clusters

One card per cluster. Each card shows:

  • the PostgreSQL version;
  • how many pods are ready (for example 3/3 ready);
  • the current primary;
  • labels such as production, PgBouncer or Backups.

Click a card to open the cluster.

Lower on the page, Recent activity lists what happened lately (for example "backup completed"). Other PostgreSQL lists databases in your Kubernetes that KeenPG does not manage yet.

docs.title: Create a cluster
docs.text:
Click Create cluster (top right). The form has 9 numbered steps. While you fill it, the Summary on the right shows what you will get.

Create cluster: project, name and version

Step 1: Project and name

  • Project: where the cluster will live. Click New… to make a new project.
  • Cluster name: lowercase letters, digits and -, for example orders-db. You can't change it later.
  • Environment: development, staging or production. This is a label that helps you sort and find clusters.
  • Description: optional, for example "orders and payments".

Step 2: PostgreSQL

  • Pick the version (15, 16, 17 or 18). Use the newest unless your application needs an older one.
  • PostGIS: pick a version only if you store maps or locations.
  • Custom image: leave it empty. KeenPG then uses its own tested image.

Create cluster: pods, size and backups

Step 3: Instances and resources

  • Encrypted storage turns on by itself when your Kubernetes has encrypting disks.
  • Pods: how many PostgreSQL servers you get.
    • 1 = a single server, with no automatic failover. Fine for testing.
    • 2 or more = one primary plus replicas, with automatic failover. Use this for production.
  • Size: click a preset (table below), or type your own values.
  • Require a different node for each pod puts each copy on a different machine, so one broken machine can't take down every copy.
Preset CPU Memory Disk Small 0.25 512 MiB 2 GiB Medium 1 2 GiB 20 GiB Large 4 8 GiB 100 GiB

Step 4: Backups

  • Keep Enable backups on. Without backups you can't restore or clone.
  • Storage: a volume (a disk inside Kubernetes) or object storage (S3, GCS, Azure). Object storage needs a credentials Secret first, from Secrets & keys.
  • Schedules use cron format, in UTC. For example, 0 1 * * 0 means every Sunday at 01:00.
    • Full: a complete copy.
    • Differential: changes since the last full backup.
    • Incremental: changes since the last backup of any type.
  • Keep full backups: how many full backups to keep. Older ones are removed automatically.

Steps 5 to 9 (optional)

Step What to set 5. Connection pooling Turn on pgBouncer if your application opens many connections. 6. Network, security, monitoring ClusterIP = reachable only inside Kubernetes. NodePort / LoadBalancer = reachable from outside. Monitoring and Logging (below). Extra image pull secrets, your own TLS certificate. 7. Users and databases Each user gets a database and a generated password. Keep Also create the postgres superuser Secret on to use the SQL editor with full rights. 8. PostgreSQL parameters Settings such as max_connections. Leave the defaults if you aren't sure. 9. Initial data Start empty, or start from another cluster's backup, optionally at a point in time.

Step 6 details: Monitoring and logging

Create cluster: Monitoring and Logging

Both are off unless you tick them:

  • Monitoring adds the collector to each pod. Metrics and slow queries go to Prometheus and show on the Grafana dashboards. It works for every PostgreSQL version. It is greyed out until monitoring is installed (kubectl apply -k config/monitoring).
  • Logging also sends the logs of PostgreSQL, Patroni, pgBackRest and pgBouncer to Loki. It needs Monitoring. It is greyed out until Loki is installed (kubectl apply -k config/logging).

You can change both later. See Monitoring and logging.

Finish

Check the Summary, optionally click View YAML to see the exact definition, then click Create cluster.

The new cluster, and a new project, show up straight away; there is no need to reload the page. It shows deploying and is usually ready in 2 to 5 minutes. The first time can take longer, because the images are downloaded.

No passwords to prepare

The Summary shows Required secrets: None needed. The operator creates every password and certificate by itself.

docs.title: Clusters list
docs.text:
Click Clusters in the menu to see every cluster of the project you picked, or of all projects.

Clusters list

Column Meaning Cluster The name. Click it to open the cluster. Status healthy, deploying, degraded or stopped. Environment The label you chose (development, production…). Instances Ready pods / total pods, for example 3/3. PostgreSQL Major version. Namespace The project of the cluster. Useful with All projects. Features Backups, PgBouncer, monitoring, logging and so on.

The list refreshes every 10 seconds, and every 5 seconds while a cluster is being created. Use the icons above the table to search, filter or choose columns.

docs.title: Inside a cluster
docs.text:
Open a cluster to see everything about it. The header shows its health, environment, project, version and current primary. The page has 8 tabs.

Cluster overview

docs.title: The tabs
docs.text: Tab What it shows and what you can do Overview Every member with its role (leader, sync_standby, replica), state and lag, the Patroni console (below), services, instance sets and the Features card. Backup & Restore Backup schedules, the list of backups, and the backup jobs. See Backup and restore. Users & databases Users the operator manages, with Connection, Edit, Add user and remove. Configuration PostgreSQL parameters and extra pg_hba access rules. Click Save to apply. Metrics Uptime, connections, cache hit rate, replication lag, database sizes and the longest-running queries. Pods & logs Every pod with its status and restarts. Logs opens a pod's log. Delete recreates a stuck pod. Events What Kubernetes and the operator reported, newest first. Look here first when something is wrong. YAML The full cluster definition. Advanced users can edit it and click Save.

docs.title: Reading the members table
docs.text:
• leader is the primary.
  • sync_standby is a replica that has every write.
  • replica is a normal copy.
  • State should be running for the leader and streaming for the others.
  • Lag of 0 B means up to date. A large, growing lag means a replica is falling behind.
flowchart LR
    L["leader<br/>state: running"] -->|"every write"| SS["sync_standby<br/>state: streaming<br/>lag: 0 B"]
    L -->|"copy"| R["replica<br/>state: streaming<br/>lag: 0 B"]
    R -.-> W{"Lag large and growing?"}
    W -->|"Yes"| BAD["Replica is falling behind"]
    W -->|"No"| GOOD["Up to date"]

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    classDef bad fill:#d04a47,stroke:#8f2c2a,color:#fff
    class SS,R,W step
    class L,GOOD ok
    class BAD bad

docs.title: The Patroni console
docs.text:
The panel under the members table runs safe Patroni commands for you. The answer appears in Output.

Button What it does list / history / show-config Show the members, past leader changes, and the current settings. switchover Moves the leader to a healthy replica, with a short pause in writes. failover Forces a new leader. Only for emergencies, when the leader is unhealthy. restart / reload Restarts a member, or reloads its settings without a restart. reinit Rebuilds a broken replica from scratch from the leader. pause / resume Turns automatic failover off and on, for planned maintenance. Rolling restart Restarts every member one by one, replicas first.

docs.title: The Actions menu
docs.text:
Click Actions (top right of the cluster page).

Actions menu

Action What happens Switchover (Patroni picks) Patroni moves the primary to the best replica. Applications reconnect within seconds. Rolling restart All pods restart one at a time, replicas first. Use it after a setting that needs a restart. Back up now (full) Starts a full backup immediately. Stop cluster Shuts down all PostgreSQL pods to save resources. Data is kept. Start cluster brings it back. Suspend reconciliation The operator stops managing this cluster: it neither changes nor repairs it. Use only for short maintenance. Resume to continue. Clone to new cluster Makes a new cluster from this one's backups. The original is not changed. Delete cluster Deletes the cluster, its disks and the backups in its volume repositories. You must type the name to confirm. This can't be undone.

Delete cluster can't be undone

It removes the disks and the backups in the volume repositories. You must type the cluster name to confirm.

docs.title: Monitoring and logging
docs.text:
Turn them on or off for a running cluster on its Overview tab, in the Features card:

Monitoring and Logging switches

The console asks first and tells you what will happen:

Turn on logging

Change What happens Monitoring on The collector is added to every pod, with pg_stat_statements for slow queries. The PostgreSQL pods restart one by one, replicas first. Monitoring off The collector is removed, and Logging goes off too. The pods restart one by one. Logging on Logs go to Loki. No restart is needed, except the very first time: the operator restarts once to turn on log collection, and each monitored cluster then needs one Rolling restart (cluster → Actions) before PostgreSQL writes its own log lines. Logging off Logs are no longer sent. Logs already in Loki stay until they expire (7 days). 
flowchart LR
    subgraph MON["Monitoring"]
        direction TB
        M1["On"] --> M2["Collector added to every pod"] --> M3["Pods restart one by one, replicas first"]
        M4["Off"] --> M5["Collector removed, Logging goes off too"] --> M6["Pods restart one by one"]
    end
    subgraph LOG["Logging"]
        direction TB
        L1["On"] --> L2["Logs go to Loki"]
        L2 -.-> L3["First time only: operator restarts once, then one Rolling restart per monitored cluster"]
        L4["Off"] --> L5["Logs no longer sent, old logs stay 7 days"]
    end
    MON --> LOG

    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    classDef warn fill:#b3760f,stroke:#7a500a,color:#fff
    classDef bad fill:#d04a47,stroke:#8f2c2a,color:#fff
    class M1,M2,M3,L1,L2 ok
    class M4,M5,M6,L4,L5 bad
    class L3 warn

Using Helm with logging?

The console turns on the operator's OpenTelemetryLogs setting the first time someone ticks Logging. A later helm upgrade sets it back to what values.yaml says. Once you use logging, put both in your values:

values.yaml
operator:
  featureGates: "OpenTelemetryMetrics=true,OpenTelemetryLogs=true"

If you forget, Observability › Dashboards shows a warning with a Turn on again button.

Older clusters

Clusters made with the old metrics exporter still work. To move them to the collector, turn Monitoring off and on.

docs.title: Connect your application
docs.text:
Open the cluster → Users & databases → Connection next to the user.

Connection details

The window shows everything an application needs. Click the copy icon next to any value.

Field Example Use Host hippo-primary.apps.svc The address of the current primary. Port 5432 The PostgreSQL port. Database / User app What to connect to, and as whom. Password (generated) Also stored in the Secret <cluster>-pguser-<user>. URI postgresql://app:…@hippo-primary.apps.svc:5432/app A complete connection string you can paste. pgBouncer host hippo-pgbouncer.apps.svc Use this instead of the host when PgBouncer is on. 
flowchart LR
    APP["Application in Kubernetes"] -->|"URI or Secret"| PRI["Primary<br/>cluster-primary"]
    APP -.->|"when PgBouncer is on"| PGB["pgBouncer host"]
    PGB --> PRI
    REP["Reports and dashboards"] -->|"read-only"| RPL["Replicas<br/>cluster-replicas.project.svc"]
    LAP["Your laptop"] -->|"kubectl port-forward"| PRI

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    classDef opt fill:#8e5bb5,stroke:#5f3a80,color:#fff
    class APP,REP,LAP step
    class PRI,RPL ok
    class PGB opt

From an application inside Kubernetes

Use the URI as shown. You can also read it from the Secret <cluster>-pguser-<user>, which has the keys host, port, user, password, dbname, uri and jdbc-uri.

For read-only traffic

For reports and dashboards, use the replicas: <cluster>-replicas.<project>.svc, same port, user and password.

From your laptop

Forward the port first:

Connect from your laptop
kubectl -n <project> port-forward svc/<cluster>-primary 5432:5432
psql "postgresql://<user>:<password>@localhost:5432/<database>"

The primary address never changes

<cluster>-primary always points to the current primary, even right after a failover. Your application doesn't need to change anything.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text:
Open Backup & Restore in the menu (or the cluster's Backup & Restore tab), and choose the cluster at the top right.

Backup and restore

What the page shows

  • Repositories and schedules: where backups go, when each type runs, and how many are kept. Click Edit to change them.
  • Backups in the repositories: every backup with its type (full, diff, incr), start time, duration, database size and backup size.
  • Backup and restore jobs: each run and whether it Succeeded.
flowchart LR
    PAGE["Backup & Restore page"] --> R["Repositories and schedules"]
    PAGE --> B["Backups in the repositories<br/>full, diff, incr"]
    PAGE --> J["Backup and restore jobs<br/>Succeeded"]
    R -->|"Edit"| R2["Change schedules and retention"]

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    class PAGE,R,B,J,R2 step

Take a backup now

Click Back up now. It appears under the jobs, then in the backup list when finished.

flowchart LR
    A["Click Back up now"] --> B["Appears under the jobs"] --> C["Shows in the backup list when finished"]

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    class A,B step
    class C ok

Restore in place

This replaces all data in this cluster with a backup.

Restore in place

  1. Click Restore in place….
  2. Choose the Repository.
  3. In Point in time, type the moment to go back to, for example 2026-11-02 10:15:00+05:30. Leave it empty to restore to the latest point possible.
  4. Click Restore. The cluster stops, restores and starts again. Changes made after that moment are lost.

Restore in place replaces all data

Changes made after the chosen moment are lost. When in doubt, use Clone to new cluster instead.

Clone to new cluster

This is the safe choice. The Create cluster form opens, already filled in, with the backup as its initial data. Pick a name and, if needed, a point in time, then click Create cluster. The original cluster is not touched.

flowchart LR
    BK["A backup"] --> I["Restore in place"]
    BK --> K["Clone to new cluster"]
    I --> I1["Replaces all data in this cluster"]
    K --> K1["New cluster is created<br/>Original is not touched"]

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    classDef bad fill:#d04a47,stroke:#8f2c2a,color:#fff
    class BK step
    class I,I1 bad
    class K,K1 ok

Use a clone to:

  • get back a table deleted by mistake: clone to just before the mistake, then copy the table back;
  • test an upgrade or a risky change;
  • give developers a copy of production.

docs.title: SQL Editor
docs.text:
Run SQL on any database straight from your browser, on the primary or on a replica.

SQL editor on a replica

Run a query

  1. Choose the Cluster, the Server and the Database at the top.
  2. Type your SQL. The left panel lists schemas, tables and views; click one to use its name.
  3. Click Run, or press F5 or Ctrl+Enter. To run only part of the text, select it first.
  4. Results appear in Data output. Click CSV (bottom right) to download them.
flowchart LR
    A["Choose Cluster, Server, Database"] --> B["Type your SQL"] --> C["Run, F5 or Ctrl+Enter"] --> D["Data output"] --> E["CSV download"]

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    class A,B,C step
    class D,E ok

Choose the server

Server list

Server Use it for Primary (read-write) The default. Everything, including changes. Any replica (read-only) Reports and heavy reads, to keep load off the primary. The replicas share the work. One instance, for example hippo-instance1-wxyz-0 (replica, read-only) Checking one exact server, for example whether a replica has the latest data.

On a replica an orange read-only label shows. Replicas are live copies, so queries that change data are refused there. The chip under the cluster tells you which server answered (leader or standby and its address).

More tools

  • Explain and Explain analyze show how PostgreSQL runs a query, to help you make it faster.
  • Messages shows notices and errors. Query history shows what you ran before.
  • + opens another query tab. Max rows limits how many rows come back.
  • The badge at the top right shows your access, for example Admin · scoped. Read-only users can only run queries that don't change data.
  • With All projects, the cluster list shows each cluster's project next to its name.

Audit log

Every query that can change data is recorded in the audit log.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
The Database manager lets you manage what is inside a cluster without writing SQL. Choose the Cluster and Database at the top right.

Database manager

The cards show the number of databases, total size, roles, open sessions, and which user the page is connected as.

Tab What you can do Databases Create, rename, change owner, drop. Roles & access Create users and groups, set passwords and expiry dates, and grant access per schema (connect / read / write / all). Schemas Create and drop schemas. Extensions Install, update or remove extensions such as pg_stat_statements. Sessions See who is connected and what they run. Cancel a query, or disconnect a session. Maintenance Run VACUUM, ANALYZE, VACUUM FULL or REINDEX, and see the largest tables with their dead rows.

Items marked cluster spec

These were created in the Create cluster form and are managed by the operator. Change those on the cluster's Users & databases tab instead.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Observability in the left menu opens two pages: Dashboards and Kubernetes.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
The Grafana dashboards of every cluster, inside the console. You don't sign in to Grafana separately: the console signs you in. Console admins are Grafana admins; everyone else can look but not change dashboards.

Dashboards

  1. Open Observability › Dashboards. Type in Search dashboards to find one.
  2. Click a dashboard. It opens on the same page, with Grafana's own time range and filters.
  3. All dashboards goes back to the list; Open in a new tab opens it on its own.
Dashboard What it shows PostgreSQL Overview All clusters at a glance. PostgreSQL Details One cluster in depth: connections, transactions, cache, locks, replication. PostgreSQL Service Health Saturation, errors and availability. Query Statistics The slowest and busiest queries (pg_stat_statements). pgBackRest Backups and WAL archiving. PGBouncer Pools, client and server connections. Pod Details CPU, memory, disk and network of each pod. Prometheus Alerts Alerts that are firing. PostgreSQL Logs The logs, coloured by level (with Logging on).

Requirements

The dashboards need monitoring installed (kubectl apply -k config/monitoring) and Monitoring on for the clusters you want to see. Users limited to some projects can't open this page, because the dashboards show every cluster.

Open Grafana on its own

Grafana lives under /grafana/:

kubectl -n keenpg-operator port-forward svc/keenpg-grafana 3000:3000     # then http://localhost:3000/grafana/

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: The health of the Kubernetes nodes and system pods under your databases.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Discovery finds other PostgreSQL databases already running in your Kubernetes that KeenPG doesn't manage.

Discovery

  • Top cards: how many databases were found, and how many are healthy or need attention.
  • PostgreSQL operators: which other operators are installed: CloudNativePG, Crunchy PGO, Percona, Zalando, StackGres, KubeDB.
  • PostgreSQL found: each database with its source (an operator, a Helm chart, a plain StatefulSet, or an external service), version, ready pods, status, primary and services. Click the arrow for details.

Discovery scans again every 30 seconds. Crunchy PGO and Percona databases can be moved into KeenPG on the Migration page.

flowchart LR
    SC["Discovery scans every 30 seconds"] --> F["Other PostgreSQL found"]
    F --> C1["Crunchy PGO"]
    F --> C2["Percona"]
    F --> C3["CloudNativePG, Zalando, StackGres, KubeDB, Helm, StatefulSet, external"]
    C1 --> MG["Move into KeenPG on the Migration page"]
    C2 --> MG

    classDef step fill:#3b82c4,stroke:#1e5a94,color:#fff
    classDef ok fill:#2e8b57,stroke:#1c5e3a,color:#fff
    classDef muted fill:#7c8794,stroke:#515a64,color:#fff
    class SC,F step
    class C1,C2,MG ok
    class C3 muted

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
Move databases from Crunchy PGO or Percona into KeenPG. KeenPG reads the source's own backups, so the source database is never changed or stopped.

Migration

  1. Open Migration and click Migrate on the cluster you want to move.
  2. Source: check the details (cluster, version, pod).
  3. Repository and backup: choose where to read backups from, and which backup. Latest means the newest backup plus every change after it.
  4. How:
    • Restore and leave for testing: builds a new KeenPG cluster from the backup. The source keeps running. Use this to test first.
    • Keep in sync: the new cluster follows the source and keeps copying its changes. When you are ready to switch, click Cut over, and the new cluster becomes a normal primary.
  5. Click Restore into a new cluster. Progress appears under Migrations.

The new cluster has the same PostgreSQL major version as the source.

docs.title: Users and access
docs.text:
Settings → Users lists everyone who can sign in to the console.

Users

  • Add user: create an account.
  • Group: decides what the person can do (table below).
  • Manage access: fine-tune one person. Allow or deny single permissions, or limit them to some projects.
  • Key icon: reset the person's password. Trash icon: remove the person.
Group Can do Admin Everything: users, access policies, settings, audit log, SQL as superuser, Grafana admin. Operator Create and run clusters, Patroni actions, backups, Secrets, Kubernetes pages, discovery and migration, SQL read/write. DBA Only the database clusters, the SQL editor (as superuser) and the database manager. No Kubernetes pages, Secrets or settings. Viewer Read only.

The Access policies tab holds rules for groups, teams or single users, optionally limited to some projects, clusters or databases. Deny wins over allow. The Administrators policy can't be changed, so an admin can never lock themselves out.

docs.title: Other pages
docs.text: Page What it is for Secrets & keys Create what some features need before you create a cluster: a registry login for private images, S3 / GCS / Azure credentials for backups, or a TLS key pair. Database passwords are not made here; the operator creates them. Operations All backup and restore jobs, and all events, for every cluster, in one list. Warning lines need attention. Settings → Projects The projects (namespaces) KeenPG uses. Add project makes a new one. Settings → Operator The operator's state and the image used for each PostgreSQL version and tool. Settings → Kubernetes Storage classes (disk types, and whether they can grow) and the nodes. Settings → Console storage The console's own small database (users, sessions, audit log) and its disk. Click Increase size if it fills up. Settings → Audit log Every change and every SQL query that changes data: when, who, what. Kept for 180 days by default.

docs.title: Upgrade the console
docs.text:
Upgrade the console
helm upgrade keenpg ./keenpg-operator -n keenpg-operator --reuse-values
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout status deploy/keenpgo-console

Then reload the browser with Ctrl+Shift+R, so it doesn't keep the old page.

  • Your users, settings, audit log, the admin password and the HTTPS certificate are kept.
  • If the image keeps the same tag (for example v6.0), make Kubernetes download it again: set the console's image pull policy to Always in your values, or run kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console.
  • Using logging? Make sure operator.featureGates still says OpenTelemetryMetrics=true,OpenTelemetryLogs=true.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text: I want to… Do this Get the admin password kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d (see Sign in) See the clusters of every project Project (top left) → All projects. Create a database for a new app Create cluster → fill steps 1–7 → Create cluster. Get my app's connection details Cluster → Users & databases → Connection. Run a report without loading the primary SQL Editor → Server → Any replica (read-only). Back up before a risky change Cluster → Actions → Back up now (full). Recover data deleted by mistake Backup & Restore → Clone to new cluster → a time just before the mistake → copy the data back. Add a replica Cluster → YAML → raise replicas under instances → Save. Change a PostgreSQL setting Cluster → Configuration → change → Save. Move the primary before maintenance Cluster → Actions → Switchover. Pause a test database to save resources Cluster → Actions → Stop cluster (data is kept). Turn on metrics or logs for a cluster Cluster → Overview → Features → Monitoring / Logging. See the dashboards Observability → Dashboards → click a dashboard. Find slow queries Observability → Dashboards → Query Statistics, or cluster → Metrics. Read a cluster's logs Observability → Dashboards → PostgreSQL Logs (Logging on). Find out why a cluster isn't healthy Cluster → Events, then Pods & logs. Give a colleague read-only access Settings → Users → Add user → group Viewer. See who changed something Settings → Audit log.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start here when something is wrong:

What you see What it means What to do Pods show ImagePullBackOff or 401 Unauthorized Kubernetes can't download the images. The registry login is missing or wrong. Run helm upgrade with pullSecret.create=true and your auth.json, then delete the stuck pods. manifest unknown / not found That image version doesn't exist in the registry. Contact KeenPG support. The browser says "Your connection is not private" The console's certificate is self-signed. Expected. Click Advanced → Continue, or trust the certificate (see HTTPS). "Wrong username or password" for admin The password is not admin: Helm made a random one. Read it from the Secret keenpgo-console-admin (see Sign in). Still wrong? Reset the admin as shown there. Console log: password authentication failed for user "keenpgo" The Secret keenpgo-console-db no longer matches the console database (for example it was deleted and made again). Put the old password back into the Secret, or give the database the new one. Ask KeenPG support for the exact commands for your case. A pod stays Pending, or a PersistentVolumeError event No disk could be created. Check Settings → Kubernetes for a storage class with free space. A MissingRequiredImage event No image is set for that PostgreSQL version. Choose a version offered in the Create cluster form. The cluster stays deploying Something is blocking the start. Read the cluster's Events tab, then Pods & logs. A replica's lag keeps growing The replica is falling behind or stuck. Overview → Patroni console → choose the member → reinit. Monitoring or Logging is greyed out Prometheus or Loki is not installed. kubectl apply -k config/monitoring (and config/logging for logs). Dashboards: "The dashboards are not available" Grafana is not installed or not reachable. kubectl apply -k config/monitoring. If Grafana runs elsewhere, set KEENPGO_GRAFANA_URL on the console. Dashboards: a panel says origin not allowed A proxy in front of the console changes the address. kubectl -n keenpg-operator set env deploy/keenpg-grafana GF_SECURITY_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=<your console address> Dashboards: "the operator has log collection turned off" A helm upgrade removed the logging setting. Click Turn on again, and add OpenTelemetryLogs=true to operator.featureGates in your values. Logging is on, but no PostgreSQL log lines (Patroni lines arrive) PostgreSQL has not restarted since log collection was turned on. Cluster → Actions → Rolling restart. SQL editor: "cannot execute … in a read-only transaction" You ran a change on a replica. Pick Primary (read-write) in Server. "No console database is configured" The console's own database isn't running. Check the pod keenpgo-console-db-0 in the keenpg-operator project.

Still stuck?

Send this output to KeenPG support:

Collect support information
kubectl -n <project> get keenpgcluster <cluster> -o yaml
kubectl -n <project> get pods,pvc,events
kubectl -n keenpg-operator logs deploy/keenpgo --tail=200
kubectl -n keenpg-operator logs deploy/keenpgo-console --tail=200

docs.title: Be careful
docs.text:
Read these before you change anything in production

  • Deleting a cluster is permanent. It removes the cluster's disks and the backups in its volume repositories. Keep important backups in object storage too, or clone before you delete.
  • Restore in place replaces all data. When in doubt, use Clone to new cluster.
  • Use 2 or more pods for production. With one pod there is no automatic failover.
  • Keep backups on. Without them you can't restore or clone.
  • Change the admin password on the first day, and never share it in chats or tickets.
  • Turning Monitoring on or off restarts the PostgreSQL pods one by one. Do it in a quiet hour for busy production databases.
  • Suspend reconciliation only for short maintenance. While suspended, the operator doesn't repair the cluster.
  • Don't delete the Secrets keenpgo-console-db or keenpgo-console-admin. The console database keeps its first password; a new Secret won't match it.

docs.title: KeenPG Console
docs.text:
The KeenPG console is a web page for running PostgreSQL on Kubernetes and OpenShift. From your browser you can create databases, connect applications, take backups and restore them, run SQL on the primary or on a replica, and watch every database on Grafana dashboards. You never need to write YAML.

This page explains every part of the console in simple words, with screenshots.

What you will learn

  • Install the console and sign in for the first time.
  • Create, monitor and manage PostgreSQL clusters.
  • Connect your application to a database.
  • Back up, restore and clone your data.
  • Run SQL, manage databases and read the dashboards.
  • Fix the most common problems.

docs.title: How the console works
docs.text:
The path of every request, from your browser to your PostgreSQL clusters:

flowchart LR
    U["1. You (browser)"] -->|"2. HTTPS"| C["3. KeenPG console"]
    C --> K["4. Kubernetes"]
    K --> O["5. KeenPG operator"]
    O --> PG["6. Your PostgreSQL clusters"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    class U,C,K,O step
    class PG ok
  1. You fill a form or press a button in the console.
  2. The console checks that you are allowed to do this. It then saves your request in Kubernetes as a KeenPGCluster object and writes an entry in the audit log.
  3. The KeenPG operator, a program running inside your Kubernetes, sees the request. It creates everything the database needs: pods, disks, network services, passwords, certificates and backup jobs.
  4. The operator keeps watching. If a pod crashes, a disk is lost or someone deletes a service by mistake, the operator puts it back.

The console and the command line always agree

For clusters, backups and settings, the console only writes the same objects you could write with kubectl. Only the SQL Editor and Databases pages talk to PostgreSQL directly, like any SQL tool.

Your databases don't depend on the console

If the console stops, your databases keep running.

Your databases don't depend on the operator either

If the operator stops, they keep running and failover still works. Only new changes wait until it is back.

docs.title: Words you will see
docs.text:
Word Meaning Project A group of databases. In Kubernetes this is a namespace, for example apps or analytics. All projects shows every project at once. Cluster One PostgreSQL database service: one primary and its replicas. Primary (also leader) The main server. All writes go here. Replica (also standby) A live copy of the primary. It can serve reads and takes over if the primary fails. Sync standby A replica that confirms every write before the primary says "done", so no data is lost if the primary fails. Failover A replica becomes the primary automatically because the primary stopped. Switchover You move the primary role to a replica on purpose, for example before maintenance. Lag How far a replica is behind the primary. 0 B means fully up to date. Patroni The tool inside each pod that chooses the primary and handles failover. pgBackRest The backup tool. Repository (repo) Where backups are kept: a disk inside Kubernetes, or object storage (S3, GCS, Azure). Point-in-time restore Restoring a database to an exact moment, for example "yesterday at 10:15". PgBouncer A connection pooler. Many application connections share a few database connections. Secret A safe place in Kubernetes for passwords, keys and certificates. Collector A small helper container added to each database pod when Monitoring is on. It collects metrics and, with Logging, the logs. Prometheus / Loki / Grafana Prometheus stores the metrics, Loki stores the logs, Grafana shows both as dashboards.

How the main parts fit together:

flowchart LR
    App["Application"] --> PB["PgBouncer"]
    PB --> P["Primary (leader)"]
    P -->|"live copy"| S["Sync standby"]
    P -->|"live copy"| R["Replica (standby)"]
    PAT["Patroni"] -. "chooses the primary" .-> P

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2937
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px,color:#1f2937

docs.title: Install with Helm
docs.text:
Already installed?

Skip this part if KeenPG is already installed for you.

Install the chart

Run this from the folder that holds the chart. It installs everything: the operator, the console and the console's own database.

Install KeenPG
helm install keenpg ./keenpg-operator -n keenpg-operator --create-namespace

Wait until all pods are Running:

Check the pods
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get pods
Expected output
NAME                                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
keenpgo-7b8d8dcc4f-tjnht            1/1     Running   0          2m
keenpgo-console-6797b94dc-rdl5j     1/1     Running   0          2m
keenpgo-console-db-0                1/1     Running   0          2m

docs.title: Open the console
docs.text:
The console service is only reachable inside Kubernetes. To open it from your browser, change the service to NodePort:

Expose the console
kubectl -n keenpg-operator patch svc keenpgo-console -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get svc keenpgo-console
Expected output
NAME              TYPE       CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)                      AGE
keenpgo-console   NodePort   10.96.120.15   <none>        80:31847/TCP,443:30512/TCP   5m

Open https://<node IP>:<node port>, for example https://192.168.49.2:30512. (On minikube, minikube ip gives the node IP.)

Certificate warning on first visit

The first time, the browser warns that the certificate is not trusted. That is expected: the console made its own certificate. Click Advanced → Continue, or see HTTPS and the certificate.

docs.title: Optional: dashboards and logs
docs.text:
Install these once if you want the Observability › Dashboards page and the Monitoring and Logging switches:

Install monitoring and logging
kubectl apply -k config/monitoring      # Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager
kubectl apply -k config/logging         # Loki, only if you want logs

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
Sign-in page

  1. Open the console address in your browser.
  2. Type your username and password, then click Sign In.

The first password

Helm makes a random password for the user admin and keeps it in the Secret keenpgo-console-admin. Read it with:

Read the admin username and password
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo
Example output
admin
x7Rk2pQw9LmZ4vTnB8sD   (yours is different)

To choose the password yourself, add --set console.admin.password='Choose-A-Password-1' to helm install.

The Secret is only read once

It is read when the console starts for the first time and there is no admin yet. After that, the password lives in the console's own database. If you change it in the console, the Secret no longer shows it.

Change the admin password on day one

Click your name (top right) → Change password.

You stay signed in for 12 hours. To sign out, click your name → Sign out.

Reset a forgotten password

Forgot the admin password?

Remove the admin user from the console database and restart the console. It then creates admin again with the password from the Secret above. Other users, the audit log and settings are kept.

flowchart LR
    A["1. Remove the admin user from the console database"] --> B["2. Restart the console"]
    B --> C["3. Console creates admin again with the password from the Secret"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    class A,B step
    class C ok
Reset the admin user
kubectl -n keenpg-operator exec keenpgo-console-db-0 -- sh -c "PGPASSWORD=\"\$POSTGRES_PASSWORD\" \$(ls -d /usr/pgsql-*/bin | tail -1)/psql -h /tmp -U keenpgo -d keenpgo -c \"DELETE FROM console_users WHERE username = 'admin';\""
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console

DELETE 1 means it worked.

Other users forgot their password? An admin resets it in Settings → Users (key icon).

docs.title: HTTPS and the certificate
docs.text:
The console always uses HTTPS. It makes its own self-signed certificate the first time it starts, and keeps it in the Secret keenpgo-console-tls.

  • Nothing else is needed: no cert-manager and no extra job. It works the same with Helm, kubectl, Argo CD and OpenShift.
  • Every console pod and every restart uses the same certificate. It is valid for 2 years; the console makes a new one 30 days before it ends.
  • http:// on the same port is sent on to https:// by itself.

Stop the browser warning

Save the certificate and trust it on your computer (it is its own authority):

Save the certificate
kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d > keenpg-console.crt

Then trust it on your system:

  • Windows

    1. Double-click the file
    2. Install Certificate
    3. Local Machine
    4. Trusted Root Certification Authorities

  • macOS

    1. Open it in Keychain Access
    2. System
    3. Set Always Trust

  • Linux (Chrome / Firefox)

    1. Browser settings
    2. Certificates
    3. Authorities
    4. Import

Advanced HTTPS setups

Your address in the certificateYour own certificateOpenShiftIngress or load balancer

By default the certificate is for the console's service names and localhost. To add the IP or name people type in the browser, set KEENPGO_TLS_HOSTS and let the console make a new certificate:

kubectl -n keenpg-operator set env deploy/keenpgo-console KEENPGO_TLS_HOSTS=192.168.49.2,console.example.com
kubectl -n keenpg-operator delete secret keenpgo-console-tls
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console

Use this for a certificate from your company's authority or cert-manager.

Put it in the same Secret. The console uses it as it is, never replaces it, and picks up a renewed one within 5 minutes:

kubectl -n keenpg-operator create secret tls keenpgo-console-tls --cert=console.crt --key=console.key \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console

Create a passthrough Route, so the browser talks HTTPS straight to the console:

oc -n keenpg-operator create route passthrough keenpgo-console --service=keenpgo-console --port=https
oc -n keenpg-operator get route keenpgo-console

Use this when an Ingress or load balancer already does HTTPS.

It can send plain HTTP to the console with the header X-Forwarded-Proto: https; the console accepts that. Or turn the console's own HTTPS off with KEENPGO_TLS=off.

docs.title: The screen layout
docs.text:
Every page has the same frame:

Area What it does Left menu Opens each page. On small screens it shows only icons; click » at the bottom to open it. Pages with an arrow (Observability) open a list of sub-pages. Project (top left) Chooses the project you are working in. All projects (the default) shows the clusters of every project you can see. Create cluster (top right) Starts a new database from any page. Your name (top right) Change your password, manage users (admins only), sign out.

Project list with All projects

Like All namespaces in OpenShift, All projects is first in the list. Pick a project to see only its clusters. The lists of clusters, the SQL editor and Backup & Restore follow the project you pick.

Your role decides what you see

You see only the pages and buttons your role allows. See Users and access.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
The Home page is your daily check: in one look you see whether everything is fine.

Home page

Top card

  • Operator ready 1/1 means the KeenPG operator is running.
  • The chips show the PostgreSQL versions you can use.
  • The four shortcuts open Create cluster, SQL editor, Databases and Migration.

Count cards

Card Meaning Clusters ring All clusters, split by state. Healthy Clusters with every pod ready. Need attention Clusters with a problem. Open them first. Being created New clusters that are still starting. Kubernetes health Problems in Kubernetes itself, for example a node that is not ready.

Your clusters

One card per cluster. Each card shows:

  • the PostgreSQL version;
  • how many pods are ready (for example 3/3 ready);
  • the current primary;
  • labels such as production, PgBouncer or Backups.

Click a card to open the cluster.

Lower on the page, Recent activity lists what happened lately (for example "backup completed"). Other PostgreSQL lists databases in your Kubernetes that KeenPG does not manage yet.

docs.title: Create a cluster
docs.text:
Click Create cluster (top right). The form has 9 numbered steps. While you fill it, the Summary on the right shows what you will get.

Create cluster: project, name and version

Step 1: Project and name

  • Project: where the cluster will live. Click New… to make a new project.
  • Cluster name: lowercase letters, digits and -, for example orders-db. You can't change it later.
  • Environment: development, staging or production. This is a label that helps you sort and find clusters.
  • Description: optional, for example "orders and payments".

Step 2: PostgreSQL

  • Pick the version (15, 16, 17 or 18). Use the newest unless your application needs an older one.
  • PostGIS: pick a version only if you store maps or locations.
  • Custom image: leave it empty. KeenPG then uses its own tested image.

Create cluster: pods, size and backups

Step 3: Instances and resources

  • Encrypted storage turns on by itself when your Kubernetes has encrypting disks.
  • Pods: how many PostgreSQL servers you get.
    • 1 = a single server, with no automatic failover. Fine for testing.
    • 2 or more = one primary plus replicas, with automatic failover. Use this for production.
  • Size: click a preset (table below), or type your own values.
  • Require a different node for each pod puts each copy on a different machine, so one broken machine can't take down every copy.
Preset CPU Memory Disk Small 0.25 512 MiB 2 GiB Medium 1 2 GiB 20 GiB Large 4 8 GiB 100 GiB

Step 4: Backups

  • Keep Enable backups on. Without backups you can't restore or clone.
  • Storage: a volume (a disk inside Kubernetes) or object storage (S3, GCS, Azure). Object storage needs a credentials Secret first, from Secrets & keys.
  • Schedules use cron format, in UTC. For example, 0 1 * * 0 means every Sunday at 01:00.
    • Full: a complete copy.
    • Differential: changes since the last full backup.
    • Incremental: changes since the last backup of any type.
  • Keep full backups: how many full backups to keep. Older ones are removed automatically.

Steps 5 to 9 (optional)

Step What to set 5. Connection pooling Turn on pgBouncer if your application opens many connections. 6. Network, security, monitoring ClusterIP = reachable only inside Kubernetes. NodePort / LoadBalancer = reachable from outside. Monitoring and Logging (below). Extra image pull secrets, your own TLS certificate. 7. Users and databases Each user gets a database and a generated password. Keep Also create the postgres superuser Secret on to use the SQL editor with full rights. 8. PostgreSQL parameters Settings such as max_connections. Leave the defaults if you aren't sure. 9. Initial data Start empty, or start from another cluster's backup, optionally at a point in time.

Step 6 details: Monitoring and logging

Create cluster: Monitoring and Logging

Both are off unless you tick them:

  • Monitoring adds the collector to each pod. Metrics and slow queries go to Prometheus and show on the Grafana dashboards. It works for every PostgreSQL version. It is greyed out until monitoring is installed (kubectl apply -k config/monitoring).
  • Logging also sends the logs of PostgreSQL, Patroni, pgBackRest and pgBouncer to Loki. It needs Monitoring. It is greyed out until Loki is installed (kubectl apply -k config/logging).

You can change both later. See Monitoring and logging.

Finish

Check the Summary, optionally click View YAML to see the exact definition, then click Create cluster.

The new cluster, and a new project, show up straight away; there is no need to reload the page. It shows deploying and is usually ready in 2 to 5 minutes. The first time can take longer, because the images are downloaded.

No passwords to prepare

The Summary shows Required secrets: None needed. The operator creates every password and certificate by itself.

docs.title: Clusters list
docs.text:
Click Clusters in the menu to see every cluster of the project you picked, or of all projects.

Clusters list

Column Meaning Cluster The name. Click it to open the cluster. Status healthy, deploying, degraded or stopped. Environment The label you chose (development, production…). Instances Ready pods / total pods, for example 3/3. PostgreSQL Major version. Namespace The project of the cluster. Useful with All projects. Features Backups, PgBouncer, monitoring, logging and so on.

The list refreshes every 10 seconds, and every 5 seconds while a cluster is being created. Use the icons above the table to search, filter or choose columns.

docs.title: Inside a cluster
docs.text:
Open a cluster to see everything about it. The header shows its health, environment, project, version and current primary. The page has 8 tabs.

Cluster overview

docs.title: The tabs
docs.text: Tab What it shows and what you can do Overview Every member with its role (leader, sync_standby, replica), state and lag, the Patroni console (below), services, instance sets and the Features card. Backup & Restore Backup schedules, the list of backups, and the backup jobs. See Backup and restore. Users & databases Users the operator manages, with Connection, Edit, Add user and remove. Configuration PostgreSQL parameters and extra pg_hba access rules. Click Save to apply. Metrics Uptime, connections, cache hit rate, replication lag, database sizes and the longest-running queries. Pods & logs Every pod with its status and restarts. Logs opens a pod's log. Delete recreates a stuck pod. Events What Kubernetes and the operator reported, newest first. Look here first when something is wrong. YAML The full cluster definition. Advanced users can edit it and click Save.

docs.title: Reading the members table
docs.text:
• leader is the primary.
  • sync_standby is a replica that has every write.
  • replica is a normal copy.
  • State should be running for the leader and streaming for the others.
  • Lag of 0 B means up to date. A large, growing lag means a replica is falling behind.
flowchart LR
    L["leader<br/>state: running"] -->|"every write"| SS["sync_standby<br/>state: streaming<br/>lag: 0 B"]
    L -->|"copy"| R["replica<br/>state: streaming<br/>lag: 0 B"]
    R -.-> W{"Lag large and growing?"}
    W -->|"Yes"| BAD["Replica is falling behind"]
    W -->|"No"| GOOD["Up to date"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    classDef bad fill:#e5393526,stroke:#e53935,stroke-width:2px
    class SS,R,W step
    class L,GOOD ok
    class BAD bad

docs.title: The Patroni console
docs.text:
The panel under the members table runs safe Patroni commands for you. The answer appears in Output.

Button What it does list / history / show-config Show the members, past leader changes, and the current settings. switchover Moves the leader to a healthy replica, with a short pause in writes. failover Forces a new leader. Only for emergencies, when the leader is unhealthy. restart / reload Restarts a member, or reloads its settings without a restart. reinit Rebuilds a broken replica from scratch from the leader. pause / resume Turns automatic failover off and on, for planned maintenance. Rolling restart Restarts every member one by one, replicas first.

docs.title: The Actions menu
docs.text:
Click Actions (top right of the cluster page).

Actions menu

Action What happens Switchover (Patroni picks) Patroni moves the primary to the best replica. Applications reconnect within seconds. Rolling restart All pods restart one at a time, replicas first. Use it after a setting that needs a restart. Back up now (full) Starts a full backup immediately. Stop cluster Shuts down all PostgreSQL pods to save resources. Data is kept. Start cluster brings it back. Suspend reconciliation The operator stops managing this cluster: it neither changes nor repairs it. Use only for short maintenance. Resume to continue. Clone to new cluster Makes a new cluster from this one's backups. The original is not changed. Delete cluster Deletes the cluster, its disks and the backups in its volume repositories. You must type the name to confirm. This can't be undone.

Delete cluster can't be undone

It removes the disks and the backups in the volume repositories. You must type the cluster name to confirm.

docs.title: Monitoring and logging
docs.text:
Turn them on or off for a running cluster on its Overview tab, in the Features card:

Monitoring and Logging switches

The console asks first and tells you what will happen:

Turn on logging

Change What happens Monitoring on The collector is added to every pod, with pg_stat_statements for slow queries. The PostgreSQL pods restart one by one, replicas first. Monitoring off The collector is removed, and Logging goes off too. The pods restart one by one. Logging on Logs go to Loki. No restart is needed, except the very first time: the operator restarts once to turn on log collection, and each monitored cluster then needs one Rolling restart (cluster → Actions) before PostgreSQL writes its own log lines. Logging off Logs are no longer sent. Logs already in Loki stay until they expire (7 days). 
flowchart LR
    subgraph MON["Monitoring"]
        direction TB
        M1["On"] --> M2["Collector added to every pod"] --> M3["Pods restart one by one, replicas first"]
        M4["Off"] --> M5["Collector removed, Logging goes off too"] --> M6["Pods restart one by one"]
    end
    subgraph LOG["Logging"]
        direction TB
        L1["On"] --> L2["Logs go to Loki"]
        L2 -.-> L3["First time only: operator restarts once, then one Rolling restart per monitored cluster"]
        L4["Off"] --> L5["Logs no longer sent, old logs stay 7 days"]
    end
    MON --> LOG
    style MON fill:#9e9e9e1a,stroke:#9e9e9e
    style LOG fill:#9e9e9e1a,stroke:#9e9e9e

    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    classDef warn fill:#fb8c0026,stroke:#fb8c00,stroke-width:2px
    classDef bad fill:#e5393526,stroke:#e53935,stroke-width:2px
    class M1,M2,M3,L1,L2 ok
    class M4,M5,M6,L4,L5 bad
    class L3 warn

Using Helm with logging?

The console turns on the operator's OpenTelemetryLogs setting the first time someone ticks Logging. A later helm upgrade sets it back to what values.yaml says. Once you use logging, put both in your values:

values.yaml
operator:
  featureGates: "OpenTelemetryMetrics=true,OpenTelemetryLogs=true"

If you forget, Observability › Dashboards shows a warning with a Turn on again button.

Older clusters

Clusters made with the old metrics exporter still work. To move them to the collector, turn Monitoring off and on.

docs.title: Connect your application
docs.text:
Open the cluster → Users & databases → Connection next to the user.

Connection details

The window shows everything an application needs. Click the copy icon next to any value.

Password (generated) Also stored in the Secret <cluster>-pguser-<user>. From an application inside Kubernetes

Use the URI as shown. You can also read it from the Secret <cluster>-pguser-<user>, which has the keys host, port, user, password, dbname, uri and jdbc-uri.

For read-only traffic

For reports and dashboards, use the replicas: <cluster>-replicas.<project>.svc, same port, user and password.

From your laptop

Forward the port first:

Connect from your laptop
kubectl -n <project> port-forward svc/<cluster>-primary 5432:5432
psql "postgresql://<user>:<password>@localhost:5432/<database>"

The primary address never changes

<cluster>-primary always points to the current primary, even right after a failover. Your application doesn't need to change anything.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text:
Open Backup & Restore in the menu (or the cluster's Backup & Restore tab), and choose the cluster at the top right.

Backup and restore

What the page shows

  • Repositories and schedules: where backups go, when each type runs, and how many are kept. Click Edit to change them.
  • Backups in the repositories: every backup with its type (full, diff, incr), start time, duration, database size and backup size.
  • Backup and restore jobs: each run and whether it Succeeded.

Take a backup now

Click Back up now. It appears under the jobs, then in the backup list when finished. Restore in place

This replaces all data in this cluster with a backup.

Restore in place

  1. Click Restore in place….
  2. Choose the Repository.
  3. In Point in time, type the moment to go back to, for example 2026-11-02 10:15:00+05:30. Leave it empty to restore to the latest point possible.
  4. Click Restore. The cluster stops, restores and starts again. Changes made after that moment are lost.

Restore in place replaces all data

Changes made after the chosen moment are lost. When in doubt, use Clone to new cluster instead.

Clone to new cluster

This is the safe choice. The Create cluster form opens, already filled in, with the backup as its initial data. Pick a name and, if needed, a point in time, then click Create cluster. The original cluster is not touched.

Use a clone to:

  • get back a table deleted by mistake: clone to just before the mistake, then copy the table back;
  • test an upgrade or a risky change;
  • give developers a copy of production.

docs.title: SQL Editor
docs.text:
Run SQL on any database straight from your browser, on the primary or on a replica.

SQL editor on a replica

Run a query

  1. Choose the Cluster, the Server and the Database at the top.
  2. Type your SQL. The left panel lists schemas, tables and views; click one to use its name.
  3. Click Run, or press F5 or Ctrl+Enter. To run only part of the text, select it first.
  4. Results appear in Data output. Click CSV (bottom right) to download them.
flowchart LR
    A["1. Choose Cluster, Server, Database"] --> B["2. Type your SQL"] --> C["3. Run, F5 or Ctrl+Enter"] --> D["4. Data output"] --> E["5. CSV download"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    class A,B,C step
    class D,E ok

Choose the server

Server list

Server Use it for Primary (read-write) The default. Everything, including changes. Any replica (read-only) Reports and heavy reads, to keep load off the primary. The replicas share the work. One instance, for example hippo-instance1-wxyz-0 (replica, read-only) Checking one exact server, for example whether a replica has the latest data.

On a replica an orange read-only label shows. Replicas are live copies, so queries that change data are refused there. The chip under the cluster tells you which server answered (leader or standby and its address).

More tools

  • Explain and Explain analyze show how PostgreSQL runs a query, to help you make it faster.
  • Messages shows notices and errors. Query history shows what you ran before.
  • + opens another query tab. Max rows limits how many rows come back.
  • The badge at the top right shows your access, for example Admin · scoped. Read-only users can only run queries that don't change data.
  • With All projects, the cluster list shows each cluster's project next to its name.

Audit log

Every query that can change data is recorded in the audit log.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
The Database manager lets you manage what is inside a cluster without writing SQL. Choose the Cluster and Database at the top right.

Database manager

The cards show the number of databases, total size, roles, open sessions, and which user the page is connected as.

Tab What you can do Databases Create, rename, change owner, drop. Roles & access Create users and groups, set passwords and expiry dates, and grant access per schema (connect / read / write / all). Schemas Create and drop schemas. Extensions Install, update or remove extensions such as pg_stat_statements. Sessions See who is connected and what they run. Cancel a query, or disconnect a session. Maintenance Run VACUUM, ANALYZE, VACUUM FULL or REINDEX, and see the largest tables with their dead rows.

Items marked cluster spec

These were created in the Create cluster form and are managed by the operator. Change those on the cluster's Users & databases tab instead.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Observability in the left menu opens two pages: Dashboards and Kubernetes.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
The Grafana dashboards of every cluster, inside the console. You don't sign in to Grafana separately: the console signs you in. Console admins are Grafana admins; everyone else can look but not change dashboards.

Dashboards

  1. Open Observability › Dashboards. Type in Search dashboards to find one.
  2. Click a dashboard. It opens on the same page, with Grafana's own time range and filters.
  3. All dashboards goes back to the list; Open in a new tab opens it on its own.
Dashboard What it shows PostgreSQL Overview All clusters at a glance. PostgreSQL Details One cluster in depth: connections, transactions, cache, locks, replication. PostgreSQL Service Health Saturation, errors and availability. Query Statistics The slowest and busiest queries (pg_stat_statements). pgBackRest Backups and WAL archiving. PGBouncer Pools, client and server connections. Pod Details CPU, memory, disk and network of each pod. Prometheus Alerts Alerts that are firing. PostgreSQL Logs The logs, coloured by level (with Logging on).

Requirements

The dashboards need monitoring installed (kubectl apply -k config/monitoring) and Monitoring on for the clusters you want to see. Users limited to some projects can't open this page, because the dashboards show every cluster.

Open Grafana on its own

Grafana lives under /grafana/:

kubectl -n keenpg-operator port-forward svc/keenpg-grafana 3000:3000     # then http://localhost:3000/grafana/

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: The health of the Kubernetes nodes and system pods under your databases.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Discovery finds other PostgreSQL databases already running in your Kubernetes that KeenPG doesn't manage.

Discovery

  • Top cards: how many databases were found, and how many are healthy or need attention.
  • PostgreSQL operators: which other operators are installed: CloudNativePG, Crunchy PGO, Percona, Zalando, StackGres, KubeDB.
  • PostgreSQL found: each database with its source (an operator, a Helm chart, a plain StatefulSet, or an external service), version, ready pods, status, primary and services. Click the arrow for details.

Discovery scans again every 30 seconds. Crunchy PGO and Percona databases can be moved into KeenPG on the Migration page.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
Move databases from Crunchy PGO or Percona into KeenPG. KeenPG reads the source's own backups, so the source database is never changed or stopped.

Migration

  1. Open Migration and click Migrate on the cluster you want to move.
  2. Source: check the details (cluster, version, pod).
  3. Repository and backup: choose where to read backups from, and which backup. Latest means the newest backup plus every change after it.
  4. How:
    • Restore and leave for testing: builds a new KeenPG cluster from the backup. The source keeps running. Use this to test first.
    • Keep in sync: the new cluster follows the source and keeps copying its changes. When you are ready to switch, click Cut over, and the new cluster becomes a normal primary.
  5. Click Restore into a new cluster. Progress appears under Migrations.

The new cluster has the same PostgreSQL major version as the source.

docs.title: Users and access
docs.text:
Settings → Users lists everyone who can sign in to the console.

Users

  • Add user: create an account.
  • Group: decides what the person can do (table below).
  • Manage access: fine-tune one person. Allow or deny single permissions, or limit them to some projects.
  • Key icon: reset the person's password. Trash icon: remove the person.
Group Can do Admin Everything: users, access policies, settings, audit log, SQL as superuser, Grafana admin. Operator Create and run clusters, Patroni actions, backups, Secrets, Kubernetes pages, discovery and migration, SQL read/write. DBA Only the database clusters, the SQL editor (as superuser) and the database manager. No Kubernetes pages, Secrets or settings. Viewer Read only.

The Access policies tab holds rules for groups, teams or single users, optionally limited to some projects, clusters or databases. Deny wins over allow. The Administrators policy can't be changed, so an admin can never lock themselves out.

docs.title: Other pages
docs.text: Page What it is for Secrets & keys Create what some features need before you create a cluster: a registry login for private images, S3 / GCS / Azure credentials for backups, or a TLS key pair. Database passwords are not made here; the operator creates them. Operations All backup and restore jobs, and all events, for every cluster, in one list. Warning lines need attention. Settings → Projects The projects (namespaces) KeenPG uses. Add project makes a new one. Settings → Operator The operator's state and the image used for each PostgreSQL version and tool. Settings → Kubernetes Storage classes (disk types, and whether they can grow) and the nodes. Settings → Console storage The console's own small database (users, sessions, audit log) and its disk. Click Increase size if it fills up. Settings → Audit log Every change and every SQL query that changes data: when, who, what. Kept for 180 days by default.

docs.title: Upgrade the console
docs.text:
Upgrade the console
helm upgrade keenpg ./keenpg-operator -n keenpg-operator --reuse-values
kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout status deploy/keenpgo-console

Then reload the browser with Ctrl+Shift+R, so it doesn't keep the old page.

  • Your users, settings, audit log, the admin password and the HTTPS certificate are kept.
  • If the image keeps the same tag (for example v6.0), make Kubernetes download it again: set the console's image pull policy to Always in your values, or run kubectl -n keenpg-operator rollout restart deploy/keenpgo-console.
  • Using logging? Make sure operator.featureGates still says OpenTelemetryMetrics=true,OpenTelemetryLogs=true.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text: I want to… Do this Get the admin password kubectl -n keenpg-operator get secret keenpgo-console-admin -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d (see Sign in) See the clusters of every project Project (top left) → All projects. Create a database for a new app Create cluster → fill steps 1–7 → Create cluster. Get my app's connection details Cluster → Users & databases → Connection. Run a report without loading the primary SQL Editor → Server → Any replica (read-only). Back up before a risky change Cluster → Actions → Back up now (full). Recover data deleted by mistake Backup & Restore → Clone to new cluster → a time just before the mistake → copy the data back. Add a replica Cluster → YAML → raise replicas under instances → Save. Change a PostgreSQL setting Cluster → Configuration → change → Save. Move the primary before maintenance Cluster → Actions → Switchover. Pause a test database to save resources Cluster → Actions → Stop cluster (data is kept). Turn on metrics or logs for a cluster Cluster → Overview → Features → Monitoring / Logging. See the dashboards Observability → Dashboards → click a dashboard. Find slow queries Observability → Dashboards → Query Statistics, or cluster → Metrics. Read a cluster's logs Observability → Dashboards → PostgreSQL Logs (Logging on). Find out why a cluster isn't healthy Cluster → Events, then Pods & logs. Give a colleague read-only access Settings → Users → Add user → group Viewer. See who changed something Settings → Audit log.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start here when something is wrong:

What you see What it means What to do Pods show ImagePullBackOff or 401 Unauthorized Kubernetes can't download the images. The registry login is missing or wrong. Run helm upgrade with pullSecret.create=true and your auth.json, then delete the stuck pods. manifest unknown / not found That image version doesn't exist in the registry. Contact KeenPG support. The browser says "Your connection is not private" The console's certificate is self-signed. Expected. Click Advanced → Continue, or trust the certificate (see HTTPS). "Wrong username or password" for admin The password is not admin: Helm made a random one. Read it from the Secret keenpgo-console-admin (see Sign in). Still wrong? Reset the admin as shown there. Console log: password authentication failed for user "keenpgo" The Secret keenpgo-console-db no longer matches the console database (for example it was deleted and made again). Put the old password back into the Secret, or give the database the new one. Ask KeenPG support for the exact commands for your case. A pod stays Pending, or a PersistentVolumeError event No disk could be created. Check Settings → Kubernetes for a storage class with free space. A MissingRequiredImage event No image is set for that PostgreSQL version. Choose a version offered in the Create cluster form. The cluster stays deploying Something is blocking the start. Read the cluster's Events tab, then Pods & logs. A replica's lag keeps growing The replica is falling behind or stuck. Overview → Patroni console → choose the member → reinit. Monitoring or Logging is greyed out Prometheus or Loki is not installed. kubectl apply -k config/monitoring (and config/logging for logs). Dashboards: "The dashboards are not available" Grafana is not installed or not reachable. kubectl apply -k config/monitoring. If Grafana runs elsewhere, set KEENPGO_GRAFANA_URL on the console. Dashboards: a panel says origin not allowed A proxy in front of the console changes the address. kubectl -n keenpg-operator set env deploy/keenpgo-grafana GF_SECURITY_CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=<your console address> Dashboards: "the operator has log collection turned off" A helm upgrade removed the logging setting. Click Turn on again, and add OpenTelemetryLogs=true to operator.featureGates in your values. Logging is on, but no PostgreSQL log lines (Patroni lines arrive) PostgreSQL has not restarted since log collection was turned on. Cluster → Actions → Rolling restart. SQL editor: "cannot execute … in a read-only transaction" You ran a change on a replica. Pick Primary (read-write) in Server. "No console database is configured" The console's own database isn't running. Check the pod keenpgo-console-db-0 in the keenpg-operator project.

Still stuck?

Send this output to KeenPG support:

Collect support information
kubectl -n <project> get keenpgcluster <cluster> -o yaml
kubectl -n <project> get pods,pvc,events
kubectl -n keenpg-operator logs deploy/keenpgo --tail=200
kubectl -n keenpg-operator logs deploy/keenpgo-console --tail=200

docs.title: Be careful
docs.text:
Read these before you change anything in production

  • Deleting a cluster is permanent. It removes the cluster's disks and the backups in its volume repositories. Keep important backups in object storage too, or clone before you delete.
  • Restore in place replaces all data. When in doubt, use Clone to new cluster.
  • Use 2 or more pods for production. With one pod there is no automatic failover.
  • Keep backups on. Without them you can't restore or clone.
  • Change the admin password on the first day, and never share it in chats or tickets.
  • Turning Monitoring on or off restarts the PostgreSQL pods one by one. Do it in a quiet hour for busy production databases.
  • Suspend reconciliation only for short maintenance. While suspended, the operator doesn't repair the cluster.
  • Don't delete the Secrets keenpgo-console-db or keenpgo-console-admin. The console database keeps its first password; a new Secret won't match it.

docs.title: KeenPG Console
docs.text:
The KeenPG console is a web page for running PostgreSQL on Kubernetes and OpenShift. From your browser you can create databases, connect applications, take backups and restore them, run SQL on the primary or on a replica, and watch every database on Grafana dashboards. You never need to write YAML.

This page explains every part of the console in simple words, with screenshots.

What you will learn

  • Install the console and sign in for the first time.
  • Create, monitor and manage PostgreSQL clusters.
  • Connect your application to a database.
  • Back up, restore and clone your data.
  • Run SQL, manage databases and read the dashboards.
  • Fix the most common problems.

docs.text:
The path of every request, from your browser to your PostgreSQL clusters:
